tests.name: Resisted Quadriceps Test
tests.procedure: Patient is seated with knee slightly flexed. Examiner applies resistance as the patient extends the knee.
tests.positiveImplication: Pain felt over anterior patella indicates patellofemoral joint irritation associated with PFPS.
tests.negativeImplication: Painless resisted knee extension.

tests.name: Step-Down Test
tests.procedure: Patient stands on a 20 cm step and slowly lowers contralateral heel to the ground while examiner observes alignment.
tests.positiveImplication: Pain over anterior knee or medial collapse (dynamic valgus) indicates PFPS and poor lower limb control.
tests.negativeImplication: Controlled, painless descent without medial knee collapse.

tests.name: Clarke’s Test (Patellar Grind Test)
tests.procedure: Patient is supine with knee extended. Examiner applies gentle downward pressure on superior pole of patella while patient contracts quadriceps.
tests.positiveImplication: Reproduction of anterior retropatellar pain indicates patellofemoral joint dysfunction.
tests.negativeImplication: Painless quadriceps contraction against patellar pressure.

tests.name: Patellar Apprehension Test
tests.procedure: Patient is supine and relaxed. Examiner pushes the patella laterally.
tests.positiveImplication: Patient shows apprehension or contracts quadriceps to prevent displacement, indicating lateral instability.
tests.negativeImplication: No apprehension or muscular guarding during lateral displacement.

tests.name: Patellar Tilt Test
tests.procedure: Patient is supine with knee extended. Examiner lifts the lateral edge of the patella.
tests.positiveImplication: Lateral patellar edge cannot reach horizontal, suggesting tight lateral retinacular structures.
tests.negativeImplication: Normal horizontal patellar tilt.

tests.name: Waldron Test
tests.procedure: Patient is seated and actively flexes and extends knee while examiner palpates patellofemoral joint.
tests.positiveImplication: Grinding, crepitus, or anterior knee pain during movement indicates patellofemoral irritation.
tests.negativeImplication: Smooth, painless active knee range of motion.

tests.name: Patellar Glide Test
tests.procedure: Patient is supine with knee extended. Examiner glides patella medially and laterally.
tests.positiveImplication: Pain or abnormal patellar mobility suggests patellar maltracking.
tests.negativeImplication: Symmetric, pain-free patellar mobility (1-2 quadrants).

tests.name: McMurray Test
tests.procedure: Patient is supine. Examiner flexes the hip and knee fully, then rotates the tibia internally and externally while extending the knee.
tests.positiveImplication: Palpable click, snap, or pain along joint line suggests medial or lateral meniscal tear.
tests.negativeImplication: Smooth, painless joint motion without joint line clicking.

tests.name: Apley’s Compression Test
tests.procedure: Patient lies prone with knee flexed to 90°. Examiner applies downward axial pressure along tibia while rotating it internally and externally.
tests.positiveImplication: Pain along joint line during compression indicates meniscal injury.
tests.negativeImplication: Painless tibial rotation under axial compression.

tests.name: Thessaly Test
tests.procedure: Patient stands on one leg with knee flexed to 20°. Patient rotates body and knee internally and externally three times.
tests.positiveImplication: Pain or locking/catching sensation along joint line suggests meniscal tear.
tests.negativeImplication: Full stable rotation without pain or mechanical locking.

tests.name: Joint Line Tenderness Test
tests.procedure: Examiner palpates along medial and lateral tibiofemoral joint lines with knee flexed to 90°.
tests.positiveImplication: Localized tenderness along joint line indicates meniscal pathology.
tests.negativeImplication: Absence of tenderness along joint line.

tests.name: Bounce Home Test
tests.procedure: Patient is supine. Examiner fully flexes the knee and then allows it to passively extend.
tests.positiveImplication: Knee does not fully extend (blocked) or produces springy end-feel, suggesting displaced meniscal fragment.
tests.negativeImplication: Complete, sharp end-feel extension without restriction.

tests.name: Ege’s Test
tests.procedure: Patient squats with knees flexed and externally rotates feet (medial meniscus) or internally rotates feet (lateral meniscus).
tests.positiveImplication: Pain or clicking along joint line during squat indicates meniscal tear.
tests.negativeImplication: Pain-free squat without joint line symptoms.

tests.name: Patella Apprehension Test
tests.procedure: Patient lies supine with knee extended. Examiner gently pushes patella laterally.
tests.positiveImplication: Apprehension, facial anxiety, or sudden quadriceps contraction indicates patellar instability.
tests.negativeImplication: Comfortable lateral displacement without guarding.

tests.name: Patella Tracking Assessment
tests.procedure: Observe patella motion during active knee flexion and extension.
tests.positiveImplication: Patella deviates laterally (J-sign) or fails to track smoothly within trochlear groove.
tests.negativeImplication: Linear vertical tracking within trochlea.

tests.name: Patellar Hypermobility Test
tests.procedure: Patient lies supine, knee extended. Examiner gently displaces patella medially and laterally.
tests.positiveImplication: Displacement greater than 2 quadrants (>50% patellar width) indicates generalized patellar laxity.
tests.negativeImplication: Displacement restricted to 1-2 quadrants.

tests.name: Q-Angle Measurement
tests.procedure: Measure angle between ASIS-to-patella center line and patella-to-tibial-tuberosity line with knee extended.
tests.positiveImplication: Increased Q-angle (>15° in men, >20° in women) indicates malalignment predisposing to dislocation.
tests.negativeImplication: Normal anatomical Q-angle.

tests.name: Observation for Patella Alta / Genu Recurvatum
tests.procedure: Inspect patellar height in full extension (Insall-Salvati ratio) and assess knee hyperextension.
tests.positiveImplication: High-riding patella (patella alta) or hyperextension (>10°) indicates structural predisposition.
tests.negativeImplication: Normal anatomical patellar position and knee extension.

tests.name: Active Straight Leg Raise Test
tests.procedure: Patient lies supine with legs extended. Examiner asks patient to lift affected leg straight up without bending knee.
tests.positiveImplication: Inability to lift leg actively indicates extensor mechanism disruption due to patellar or tibial fracture.
tests.negativeImplication: Ability to perform active straight leg raise.

tests.name: Patellar Tap / Palpation Test
tests.procedure: Patient lies supine with knee relaxed. Examiner palpates patella gently feeling for gap, step-off, or bone fragment displacement.
tests.positiveImplication: Palpable defect, separation, or severe localized tenderness indicates displaced patella fracture.
tests.negativeImplication: Intact patellar contour without palpable gap.

tests.name: Ottawa Knee Rules Assessment
tests.procedure: Assess age (≥55), isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, flexion <90°, or inability to bear weight 4 steps.
tests.positiveImplication: Positive criteria indicate immediate radiographic evaluation requirement.
tests.negativeImplication: Negative criteria reliably rule out knee fracture without radiography.

tests.name: Tibial Plateau Palpation Test
tests.procedure: Palpate medial and lateral tibial condyles and tibial plateau margins.
tests.positiveImplication: Focal acute bony tenderness suggests tibial plateau fracture.
tests.negativeImplication: Absence of acute focal bony tenderness.

tests.name: Noble’s Compression Test
tests.procedure: Patient lies supine. Examiner flexes knee to 90° and applies pressure over lateral femoral epicondyle while slowly extending knee.
tests.positiveImplication: Reproduction of pain over lateral femoral epicondyle at approximately 30° flexion indicates ITBS.
tests.negativeImplication: Painless knee extension under epicondylar pressure.

tests.name: Ober’s Test
tests.procedure: Patient lies on unaffected side. Examiner extends and abducts hip, then slowly lowers the leg into adduction.
tests.positiveImplication: Leg remains abducted and does not drop below horizontal, indicating contracture/tightness of iliotibial band.
tests.negativeImplication: Thigh drops below horizontal into smooth adduction.

tests.name: Renne’s Test
tests.procedure: Patient stands on affected leg and performs single-leg squat while examiner applies pressure over lateral femoral epicondyle.
tests.positiveImplication: Pain over lateral femoral epicondyle at 30°–40° of knee flexion confirms ITBS.
tests.negativeImplication: Painless single-leg squat.

tests.name: Modified Thomas Test
tests.procedure: Patient lies supine at edge of table, hugging contralateral knee to chest. Examiner assesses affected thigh position.
tests.positiveImplication: Thigh remains abducted and externally rotated, indicating lateral soft tissue tightness.
tests.negativeImplication: Thigh rests flat on table in neutral alignment.

tests.name: Lateral Epicondyle Palpation Test
tests.procedure: Examiner palpates lateral femoral epicondyle with knee moved between 0° and 90° flexion.
tests.positiveImplication: Sharp localized tenderness over lateral epicondyle, maximal at 30° flexion, indicates ITBS.
tests.negativeImplication: Absence of lateral epicondylar tenderness.

tests.name: Patellar Tendon Palpation Test

tests.positiveImplication: Point tenderness at inferior pole (Basset’s sign) that diminishes in flexion confirms tendinopathy.
tests.negativeImplication: Absence of tenderness along patellar tendon.

tests.name: Single-Leg Hop Test
tests.procedure: Patient performs repeated hops on the affected leg.
tests.positiveImplication: Reproduction of localized pain at patellar tendon during high-rate loading.
tests.negativeImplication: Painless hopping on affected leg.

tests.name: Pes Anserinus Palpation Test
tests.procedure: Patient lies supine with knee extended. Examiner palpates anteromedial proximal tibia, 5–7 cm below medial joint line.
tests.positiveImplication: Focal localized tenderness over pes anserine bursa indicates bursitis.
tests.negativeImplication: No tenderness at pes anserine insertion.

tests.name: Resisted Knee Flexion Test
tests.procedure: Patient flexes knee from 90° while examiner applies manual resistance.
tests.positiveImplication: Pain at pes anserinus region indicates tendon/bursal irritation.
tests.negativeImplication: Painless resisted knee flexion.

tests.name: Resisted Hip Adduction Test
tests.procedure: Patient performs hip adduction against examiner resistance.
tests.positiveImplication: Pain at medial proximal tibia insertion confirms gracilis/pes anserine involvement.
tests.negativeImplication: Painless resisted hip adduction.

tests.name: Hamstring Stretch Test
tests.procedure: Examiner passively extends knee with hip flexed, stretching hamstring tendons.
tests.positiveImplication: Pain at pes anserinus region during passive stretch.
tests.negativeImplication: Normal hamstring excursion without localized insertion pain.

tests.name: Joint Line Differentiation Test
tests.procedure: Examiner palpates medial joint line and pes anserine region sequentially.
tests.positiveImplication: Tenderness strictly 5-7 cm below joint line (pes anserinus) with negative joint line tenderness excludes meniscal tear.
tests.negativeImplication: Tenderness on joint line suggests meniscal pathology rather than bursitis.

tests.name: Wilson’s Test
tests.procedure: Patient lies supine. Examiner flexes knee to 90°. Patient actively extends knee while examiner internally rotates tibia.
tests.positiveImplication: Pain between 30°–40° extension relieved immediately by external tibial rotation indicates OCD of medial femoral condyle.
tests.negativeImplication: No pain during internal rotation extension.

tests.name: Passive Condylar Palpation Test
tests.procedure: Patient knee flexed to 90°. Examiner palpates femoral condyles directly through flexed joint.
tests.positiveImplication: Focal articular tenderness over femoral condyle indicates OCD lesion.
tests.negativeImplication: Absence of condylar tenderness.

tests.name: Joint Effusion Test (Stroke Test)
tests.procedure: Examiner strokes medial knee upward and lateral knee downward to evaluate fluid bulge.
tests.positiveImplication: Fluid wave or bulge indicates joint effusion associated with OCD lesion.
tests.negativeImplication: Zero intra-articular fluid wave.

tests.name: Single-Leg Squat Loading Test
tests.procedure: Patient performs single-leg squat on affected leg.
tests.positiveImplication: Deep, poorly localized articular pain indicates articular surface pathology.
tests.negativeImplication: Painless single-leg squat.

tests.name: Foucher’s Sign
tests.procedure: Patient lies supine. Examiner palpates popliteal mass with knee fully extended, then with knee flexed to 45°.
tests.positiveImplication: Popliteal mass becomes firm/tense in full extension and softens or disappears in flexion, confirming Baker’s cyst.
tests.negativeImplication: Mass does not alter consistency with joint angle (consider solid tumor).

tests.name: Popliteal Palpation Test
tests.procedure: Examiner palpates medial aspect of popliteal fossa between semimembranosus and medial gastrocnemius head.
tests.positiveImplication: Smooth, tense, fluctuant fluid-filled mass indicates popliteal cyst.
tests.negativeImplication: Empty popliteal fossa without palpable mass.

tests.name: Transillumination Test
tests.procedure: Light source placed against posterior knee swelling in a dimmed examination room.
tests.positiveImplication: Light transilluminates through mass, confirming fluid content rather than solid tissue.
tests.negativeImplication: Opaque mass failing to transilluminate.

tests.name: Knee Effusion Stroke Test
tests.procedure: Examiner performs sweep/stroke test across medial and lateral parapatellar gutters.
tests.positiveImplication: Associated joint effusion present, confirming intra-articular pathology feeding the cyst.
tests.negativeImplication: No intra-articular effusion.

tests.name: Passive Joint Motion Test
tests.procedure: Examiner gently moves patient’s knee through minimal passive flexion and extension.
tests.positiveImplication: Severe, excruciating pain with even minimal passive motion indicates acute septic or acute inflammatory arthritis.
tests.negativeImplication: Tolerable joint motion.

tests.name: Local Temperature Assessment
tests.procedure: Examiner uses dorsum of hand to compare skin temperature of affected knee to contralateral knee.
tests.positiveImplication: Marked erythema and localized calor (significantly elevated temperature) indicate acute infection/inflammation.
tests.negativeImplication: Normothermic joint surface.

tests.name: Joint Effusion Test (Bulge / Ballottement Test)
tests.procedure: Examiner applies downward pressure on suprapatellar pouch and ballottes patella against femur.
tests.positiveImplication: Tense joint effusion with floating patella indicates large intra-articular inflammatory/purulent fluid collection.
tests.negativeImplication: Absence of ballottement or effusion wave.

tests.name: Diagnostic Arthrocentesis (Gold Standard)
tests.procedure: Sterile needle joint aspiration for synovial fluid WBC count, Gram stain, crystals, and culture.
tests.positiveImplication: Cloudy/purulent fluid with WBC >50,000/µL and positive Gram stain/culture confirms septic arthritis.
tests.negativeImplication: Clear fluid with normal cell count.
